speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is about whether every worker gets a fair chance to stand back up after a fall.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Over the years, I have spoken in this House about preventing workplace fatalities, strengthening safety culture and improving near-miss reporting.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But while we have invested heavily in preventing injuries, we must now invest just as seriously in what happens after.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Because for many workers, that is when the real struggle begins.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Behind each number is a worker and a family, relieved that a life was not lost, but with deep anxiety about recovery, about income and whether life can return to normal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And this challenge is not limited to workplace injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We are seeing more serious health conditions affecting working-age Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A recent report highlighted rising stroke cases among those in their 30s – people who are in the prime of their working lives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Whether from injury or illness, the pattern is the same.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The longer a worker stays away from work, the harder it becomes to return.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is dignity, purpose and a sense of belonging.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: That is why return-to-work must be treated as a core pillar of our workforce system, not a secondary consideration.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we look at leading jurisdictions, there is a clear lesson for us.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The most effective systems do not wait for full recovery.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the Netherlands, employers and injured workers have clear duties, where such workers are actively reintegrated through structured plans, medical support and suitable work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Australia and New Zealand, return-to-work is embedded early, with work capacity assessments and coordinated rehabilitation support involving employers, insurers, public agencies and healthcare professionals to support workplace reintegration.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Sweden, the Social Insurance Agency coordinates support for workers returning to employment after prolonged illness.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Employers ensure workplace adaptation and plan for return-to-work, while workers who cannot return to their previous jobs are further supported by various agencies through skills training, vocational rehabilitation and job matching aligned with their work capacity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Across these systems, three principles stand out: early intervention, shared responsibility and workplace-centred solutions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Singapore has made good progress in this area.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But we can and we should take the next step forward.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, we must intervene earlier and more systematically.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Studies show that having structured systems in place to deliver return-to-work sooner is a strong determinant of whether a worker successfully reintegrates at their workplace to contribute productively and without feeling excluded.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: International evidence shows that the first few weeks after an injury or illness are critical.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we miss the window, we lose the worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If support comes too late, workers risk drifting into long-term absence from the workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, while Singapore has return-to-work programmes, activation may not always happen early enough or consistently across sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is because participation is voluntary and largely dependent on employer willingness.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should therefore strengthen early intervention by encouraging earlier referral into return-to-work support; establishing clearer expectations for employer engagement; and promoting early coordination between employers, workers, insurers and healthcare practitioners.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we act earlier, we can significantly improve outcomes for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am therefore glad that the forthcoming Alliance for Action on Safety and Health for Employment Longevity intends to explore industry-led solutions to promote return-to-work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) stands ready to support this effort.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, we must strengthen employer capability, especially amongst small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If they are not equipped to support return-to-work, many workers will fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In short, if return-to-work does not work for SMEs, it does not work for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many employers want to help but may not know how.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In leading jurisdictions, employers are supported with clear frameworks, practical tools and access to return-to-work coordinators.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Singapore, NTUC, together with the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF), is developing the Tripartite Advisory on Providing Reasonable Accommodations to Persons with Disabilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider expanding this advisory or, perhaps, introducing a complementary one – to explicitly cover workers recovering from injuries and serious health conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This should include practical guidance on job redesign and phased return; workplace adjustments and assistive solutions; and managing productivity during recovery.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should also explore a shared return-to-work support model and increase awareness and access for SMEs to trained coordinators or centralised expertise.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will ensure that smaller firms are not disadvantaged in supporting their workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Third, we must support workers who are unable to return to their previous roles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For some workers, especially after serious injury or illness, returning to the same job may no longer be possible.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Without structured support, these workers risk long-term unemployment and loss of livelihood.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A worker who cannot return to the same job should not be left without a future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Canada and parts of Europe, workers are supported through vocational rehabilitation, retraining and job matching based on their work capacities, post-injury.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This ensures they remain active contributors to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, SG Enable offers both job placement and job support services, which provide coaching, job matching and workplace support to help persons with disabilities enter and remain in employment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will ensure that a health setback does not become a permanent setback.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, support pathways are strongest for work-related injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But for workers recovering from serious non-work-related conditions, support remains uneven today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: From the worker's perspective, there is no difference between a workplace injury and a serious illness – only the question of whether they can return to work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The impact is the same: loss of income, reduced work capacity and uncertainty about the future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In countries, like New Zealand, support is structured around recovery and work capacity – not just the cause of injury.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unlike support for persons with disabilities, there is currently no dedicated funding mechanism to incentivise employers to provide workplace accommodations for workers returning to work after serious non-work-related illnesses or medical conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Therefore, such a time-bound scheme could help to offset productivity adjustments and accommodation costs as workers gradually regain work capacity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At the same time, we should reduce financial barriers for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These would ease out-of-pocket costs and support the worker's recovery.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Fairness must not depend on how a worker fell ill or got injured.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It must depend on our commitment to help them recover.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A strong return-to-work system can make the difference between recovery and long-term exclusion.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As our workforce ages and working lives lengthen, such challenges will become more commonplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must therefore act with urgency and with purpose.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A fair society is not judged only by how it protects our workers from harm – but by how we help them recover when harm occurs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us build a system where recovery does not end at discharge, but leads back to work, to dignity and a second chance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Because at NTUC, we strongly believe that Every Worker Matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Indeed, efforts to strengthen workplace safety and health are not limited to prevention and enforcement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: They include helping workers to maintain or re-enter employment after a serious injury or health episode.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Notwithstanding Singapore's record low fatal and major injury rates, MOM is keenly aware that there are also workers who experience health-related setbacks or other types of injuries that impact their functional capacity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: As people live longer and have longer working lives, it will become increasingly important to support individuals through their careers, including during periods of recovery from injury or ill health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: These jobseekers have the potential to regain meaningful employment, if given appropriate and adequate support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: MOM therefore shares Mr Yong's interest in strengthening return-to-work pathways, which can contribute to workforce well-being and productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: When implemented effectively, all stakeholders stand to gain.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Return-to-work services aim to support individuals as they resume employment after illness or injury, in a safe and sustainable manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This requires vocational rehabilitation and coordination across healthcare providers, employers and workers, and involves personalised plans based on functional ability and job requirements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: For workers, this reduces the risk of re-injury or relapse and facilitates psychological readiness to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It also provides income security and prevents early attrition from the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: For employers, effective return-to-work policies not only demonstrate a genuine commitment to employee well-being but also safeguards valuable human capital by retaining trained and experienced workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: There are different pathways to return to employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: One could return to the same role with the same employer, and with modifications to support the recovery process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Alternatively, the worker could return to the same employer but undertake a different role more suited to his or her current capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Or, as the Member had mentioned, some workers may need to be matched with a different organisation or consider a new career path.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Beyond medical treatment and rehabilitative therapy, MOM recognises that workplaces play a crucial role too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Success hinges on having workplaces that are committed to facilitating workers' reintegration – recognising workers' strengths and enabling them to fulfil their potential at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This means fostering a supportive workplace culture and implementing practical accommodations, so that workers can perform their roles effectively despite their limitations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Over the years, MOM had worked with our partners to strengthen the spectrum of return-to-work pathways in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: To support workers returning to their previous employment after a work injury, MOM conducted a pilot with the Workplace Safety and Health Council (WSHC) from 2017 to 2021 to establish return-to-work capabilities in seven public hospitals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Back then, MOM observed that return-to-work services were typically limited to multinational corporations with in-house capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We worked with hospitals to develop workflows and to train coordinators to support injured workers in navigating them back to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Besides undergoing occupational therapy and rehabilitation, workers received support from coordinators who engaged their employers on implementing a customised return-to-work plan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: With the experience from the pilot, hospitals continue to offer return-to-work services today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: For work-related injuries, such return-to-work expenses are claimable under the Work Injury Compensation Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We agree with the Member that beyond this group of workers resuming their previous employment after a workplace injury, return-to-work pathways should be made more available to other workers facing non-work-related conditions or who cannot return to their previous jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The pilot involved a partnership between Workforce Singapore and the Public Health Institutions, targeting workers who were recovering from a recent health setback and had been assessed as fit to re-enter the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Participating workers received personalised career coaching services, alongside targeted health advisory and emotional support from medical and community social workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Coordination between career coaches and social workers was facilitated through a shared case management platform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Following the Bounce Back Lab pilot, healthcare clusters have implemented processes to strengthen integrated healthcare and employment support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Additionally, the healthcare clusters have fostered partnerships with organisations beyond Workforce Singapore to provide a wider range of referral options for patients seeking employment support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The pilots I have highlighted set forth our initial efforts to lay the foundation for return-to-work ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Even so, MOM recognises that more can be done, including through learning from best practices in other countries, as suggested by Mr Yong.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: First, we can do more to raise awareness and utilisation of existing return-to-work services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: For example, the hospitals' return-to-work programmes provide an established and proven pathway to support workers in returning to their former employment post-injury.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Greater awareness of these programmes among healthcare professionals, workers and employers would facilitate early intervention, which is important for workers to return to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Second, to remain effective, return-to-work service providers must strengthen their competencies to better integrate workers' safety and health needs with employment support, especially as our workforce composition and working conditions evolve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: For example, familiarity with industry-specific job tasks and new assistive technologies would enable service providers to better engage employers on job redesign and modification.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Third, we can better encourage and equip employers, especially SMEs, to implement practical work accommodations for recovering workers to support their gradual resumption of work responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: As a first step, MOM is looking to partner with the industry and crowdsource innovative ideas to improve return-to-work outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We encourage the public to participate in these ground-up solutions later in the year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Promising prototypes can be scaled for wider adoption, while insights from the AfA process will also inform our policy reviews.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: While there are areas for improvement, I would like to acknowledge the current return-to-work efforts of our healthcare professionals, career and employment agencies, employers, unions and workers themselves, who have contributed to helping workers overcome health-related setbacks, so that they can continue on their career journeys.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Ultimately, further strengthening return-to-work pathways will require the commitment of all relevant stakeholders in the ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Let us continue working together to maximise the employment potential and longevity of all workers, a thriving economy and an inclusive Singapore.
